teaser: A severed head floats in a palace, and only one person in the room can see it.
review_notes:
Moreau stayed away from the Salon from 1869 to 1876 after harsh reviews: check.
This Orsay work is the watercolor shown at the 1876 Salon, about 106 x 72 cm: check.
Identification of the shadowed figures at left as Herod and Herodias follows the usual reading.
Architecture inspired by the Alhambra, known to Moreau through photographs and prints: check.
The dark stain on the floor is read here as blood.

lesson.text: In 1869 the Paris critics tore into Gustave Moreau. His two big canvases at the Salon, the official yearly exhibition, were called strange, cold and overloaded. He took it badly. He shut the door of his studio and did not show a single work at the Salon for seven years.

When he came back in 1876, he was 50 and had spent those years on one story: Salome, the princess whose dance cost John the Baptist his head. He sent an oil painting of the dance, and this picture, which shows what comes after. Crowds gathered in front of both.

The Bible tells it in a few lines. King Herod, delighted by the dancing of his stepdaughter, promises her anything she wants. Pushed by her mother Herodias, she asks for the head of the prophet John, who is in the king's prison. The Gospels do not even give her name.

Painters before Moreau showed the head on a platter, served like a dish. He does something no text describes. The head rises into the air, dripping, inside a blaze of light, and stares straight at the dancer.

lesson.title: Dancer and prophet
lesson.text: The picture is a duel between two faces, with an arm stretched between them.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: John's head hangs in mid-air inside a double halo, a gold ring and then a burst of white rays. His eyes are open and fixed on Salome. Dark blood runs down from the neck.

spots.title: Salome's face
spots.text: She has stopped mid-step. Her head turns toward the vision under a tall jeweled headdress, her eyes level with it. She does not scream or back away.

spots.title: The arm
spots.text: Her left arm, heavy with bracelets, shoots out with the palm open. Is she pointing, accusing, or trying to push the thing away? Moreau leaves all three possible.

lesson.text: So is the head really there? Check the other people in the hall. If a glowing, bleeding head appeared above the floor, you would expect someone to react.

Nobody does. The guard looks elsewhere, the musician stares ahead, the king sits still. The apparition exists for Salome alone. Moreau has painted the inside of a mind: guilt, or fear, or desire, made visible in a room where everything else stays calm.

This is not an oil painting. It is a watercolor on paper, over a meter tall (106 x 72 cm, about 42 x 28 in), an unusually large size for the medium. Moreau built it up with touches as fine as embroidery, then scratched and heightened the surface for the glints of jewelry.
Three lines hold this crowded picture together.

lines.label: The accusation
lines.text: From Salome's shoulder along her arm and on to the head: a single rising line joins the killer to the victim. Your eye cannot avoid traveling it.

lines.label: The fall of blood
lines.text: Blood drops straight down from the neck to the floor. It is the only truly vertical action in the scene, and it pins the floating head to the ground.

lines.label: The stain
lines.text: On the pale floor, a long dark red pool spreads. A vision should not bleed on real paving stones. Moreau blurs the border between dream and fact on purpose.

lesson.text: That pool on the floor is the unsettling part. If the head is only in her imagination, the stain should not be there. Moreau refuses to settle it, and that refusal is exactly what the next generation of artists loved in him.

The setting adds to the spell. Moreau never traveled to the Middle East. He assembled this palace at his desk from photographs, prints and museum objects: a Moorish arch like those of the Alhambra in Spain, columns covered in patterns, costumes from India and Persia, all mixed freely.

Moreau prepared his Salome pictures like a novelist researching a book. He filled sheet after sheet with studies of the dancer's pose, her jewels, the columns and the guard, drawing some figures from live models and copying ornaments from magazines and museum cases.
Symbolism, the movement Moreau helped start, uses a visible scene to show an invisible one. The subject here is not a beheading. It is what goes on inside Salome afterward.

spots.title: The executioner
spots.text: A guard stands at the right with his sword, a red cloth around his hips and his face half wrapped. He did the deed, yet the head floating beside him does not make him turn.

spots.title: The platter
spots.text: A shallow dish lies on the floor near the guard's bare feet. It is the platter of the old story, set aside, now that the head has left it.

spots.title: The musician
spots.text: A veiled young woman sits with her instrument, eyes forward, hands still. The music has stopped but she has noticed nothing.

spots.title: The royal couple
spots.text: In the shadow at the left sit the ones who wanted this death, with a turbaned figure standing behind. Moreau keeps them dim so the drama stays between two faces.

spots.title: The costume
spots.text: Salome wears almost nothing but jewels: chains, belts and a veil stitched with stones that trails to the floor. Moreau draws them bead by bead.

spots.title: The column
spots.text: Blue and gold patterns cover the capital, the carved top of the column. The whole hall is treated like a jewel box.

spots.title: Fallen flowers
spots.text: Petals and blossoms lie scattered on the paving in the corner, the leftovers of the feast and the dance.

lesson.text: Among the first admirers was the novelist Joris-Karl Huysmans. In his 1884 book Against Nature, the hero buys Moreau's two Salome pictures and spends pages describing them. The novel became a cult object, and Salome became the obsession of the 1890s.

Oscar Wilde knew those pages. In 1891 he wrote his play Salome, in French, and gave the princess a will of her own: in his version she asks for the head because she wants the prophet, not because her mother tells her to.

The man who had hidden from the critics ended up as a professor at the national art school in Paris. His students included Henri Matisse and Georges Rouault. He told them to trust their imagination, which is what seven years of silence had taught him.

quiz.question: What did Moreau do after the harsh reviews of 1869?
options: He stayed away from the Salon for seven years
He gave up painting for sculpture
quiz.explanation: He did not exhibit at the Salon again until 1876.

quiz.question: Who in the picture sees the floating head?
quiz.explanation: The other figures do not react at all.

quiz.question: What is The Apparition made with?
quiz.explanation: It is a large watercolor, over a meter tall.

quiz.question: Which detail blurs the line between vision and reality?
options: The pool of blood on the floor
quiz.explanation: A vision should not leave a stain on the paving.

quiz.question: Which novelist described Moreau's Salome pictures at length in 1884?
quiz.explanation: His hero in Against Nature owns both pictures.

quiz.question: How did Moreau come up with the palace?
options: He combined photographs, prints and museum objects
He painted it on site in Jerusalem
He copied a stage set from an opera
quiz.explanation: He never traveled to the Middle East.

facts.text: The Gospels describe John the Baptist's head floating in the air.
facts.explanation: The floating head is Moreau's invention; the texts mention only a platter.

facts.text: Henri Matisse was one of Moreau's students.
facts.explanation: Moreau taught Matisse and Rouault in Paris.

facts.text: Moreau painted the palace during a long stay in the Middle East.
facts.explanation: He never went there and worked from photographs and prints.
